passage: Uday, I heard you tell the client 'Oh, it was the team, not me' three times today. Let me tell you what I did at your age. At twenty-five I worked at a publishing house, and every compliment I got, I swatted away. 'It was nothing.' 'Anyone could.' My editor, an old Parsi lady named Mrs Kapadia, finally said, 'Pallavi, when someone gives you a gift, you don't throw it back. You say thank you.' So I practised. Just 'thank you'. Nothing after it. It felt like standing in the rain without an umbrella. I also kept a small notebook in my drawer: one line for every good thing that happened at work. Thirty years later I have eleven notebooks. On bad days I read one. So tomorrow, when the client praises your work, try it. Two words.

qa.q: How many notebooks does Pallavi have now?
qa.a: Pallavi has eleven notebooks.

qa.q: Why did saying just 'thank you' feel like standing in the rain without an umbrella?
qa.a: Without an excuse to hide behind, Pallavi felt exposed; accepting praise plainly meant letting the good thing count, which felt unfamiliar and a little unsafe.

qa.q: What two habits does Pallavi suggest, and why might they help Uday?
qa.a: Saying just 'thank you' lets praise land, and a private notebook of good moments gives steady evidence to read on bad days, building confidence instead of doubt.

qa.q: How might the client feel if Uday simply says 'thank you'?
qa.a: The client would likely feel the compliment was received, and may trust Uday's work more than when the praise was pushed onto the team.

grounding: Shows a senior colleague recalling how they learned to simply thank people for compliments and keep notebooks of achievements, and passing it on.

'This is the best design this town has seen. You thought of the children's corner nobody else did.' Her old answer was already on her tongue: 'Oh, it's the team, really.' She stopped it. 'Thank you,' she said. Just that. It felt strange, like leaving a door open. In the auto back, rain dripping from her dupatta, she opened the note on her phone titled 'Things that went right' and typed: '12 Aug. Client praised children's corner. Said thank you. Didn't argue.' It was the thirty-first entry.

passage: At the end of the Saturday rush in the Jayanagar café, Shankar, the owner, leaned into the kitchen. 'Madhav, that new ragi dosa. Three tables asked who made it.' Madhav wiped his hands and felt the usual words rise: it was a fluke, the batter just turned out well. Instead he said, 'Thank you. I worked on it all week.' Shankar nodded and went back out. That was it. No argument, no shrinking. Madhav stood there a moment, surprised by how quiet it was. That night in his rented room he took out the thin notebook he kept under the mattress and wrote the date and one line: 'Ragi dosa. Three tables asked.' Above it were other lines: the first day he ran the grill alone, the regular who asked for him by name. He read them twice before switching off the light.

Omkar opened his mouth. The old words were ready: It's just the masala, anyone can make it.

"...Thank you, dada."

Tushar raised an eyebrow. "That's it? No 'it's nothing'?"

"I'm practising." Omkar laughed a little. "My manager said I argue with every compliment. She said it makes people feel stupid for praising me."

"Your manager's smart."

"So I just say thank you. It feels weird. Like wearing someone else's shirt."

Omkar hesitated, then took out his phone. "I keep a list. Things I did that went well. The client pitch in March. Fixing Aai's leaking tap. Running 5K. Today I'll add: pav bhaji, Tushar approved."

Tushar laughed. "Put it in capitals."

Omkar typed it. Then he took a second helping without apologising for it.

passage:
I'm Vinita. Until last year, if anyone praised my work, I had a reflex: "Oh, it was the team." "It was easy." "I just got lucky." My friend told me it was actually exhausting to watch. "You're a brilliant woman who talks like a nervous intern," she said.

So in January I made two small rules.

One: when someone compliments me, I say "thank you" and nothing else. No explaining it away.

Two: I keep a private note on my phone called "Things that went well." Just facts.

The first test came in February. Tejas, our senior analyst, stopped by my desk and said, "Your flood-risk report was the clearest one we've had." My mouth started to say "the data was easy." I bit it back. "Thank you." He nodded and left. My heart was pounding, which is ridiculous.

That night I wrote it in the note. There are thirty-one things on it now. On bad days I scroll through it. It doesn't make me arrogant. It makes me steadier.

qa.q: How many things are on Vinita's note now?
qa.a: There are thirty-one things on it now.

qa.q: Why was Vinita's heart pounding when she simply said "thank you"?
qa.a: Accepting praise without deflecting felt risky and unfamiliar, as if she were claiming too much. Breaking a long habit, even a small one, felt big.

qa.q: What does Vinita's approach show about letting good things count?
qa.a: Saying thank you and recording facts helped her confidence rest on evidence rather than doubt. She says it makes her steadier, not arrogant.

qa.q: How might Tejas have experienced Vinita's simple "thank you"?
qa.a: Tejas probably felt his compliment was received, which is pleasant for the person giving it. If she'd argued, he might have felt awkward for praising her.

grounding: A young woman practises simply thanking people for compliments and keeps a private list of achievements, which steadies her confidence.

Himani and I have been working on something small. When the regional head praised her training session in Monday's meeting, the old Himani would have said, 'Oh, it was mostly the slides,' and looked at the table. This time she said, 'Thank you. I worked hard on that.' Then she stopped. I watched her hands grip the pen for a second, as if saying it cost her something. Afterwards she showed me the notebook she has started keeping, as we discussed: a private list of wins. It has eleven entries so far, including 'fixed the billing bug', 'calmed an angry client' and now 'training session, praised by regional head'. She said reading it on Sunday evenings makes Monday feel less shaky. Next step: I'll ask her to present the list herself at her mid-year review, in her own words.
Dilnaz

Today Shreya from the English department stopped me in the corridor and said the choir's assembly song was the best thing she'd heard all term. I felt the old words rising: 'It was the kids, not me. Tonight I opened the 'Wins' page at the back of this diary. It's a month since I started it. Fourteen lines now. Added: 'Assembly song. Shreya said best of term. I said thank you.' Ujjwal

At the government school in a village near Kolhapur, the block education officer visited Parveen's Class 3 and said, "Your children read better than any class in the block." Parveen felt the old words rise, "Oh no, it's the children, not me," and swallowed them.

"Thank you," she said instead. Her ears went hot. It felt almost rude.

After school she told her friend Ira, who taught next door. Ira grinned. "And the list?"

Parveen pulled out the small notebook she had started in January. On the first page: "Rekha read a whole story aloud." "Parents' meeting: 30 came." Now she added: "Officer: best readers in the block."

Some evenings, when the old doubt came, I'm not a real teacher, she read the notebook from the start. It didn't make the doubt vanish. But it gave the doubt something to argue with.

passage:
After Hana's first presentation to the design team in Cairo, Jamal caught her in the corridor. "That was really clear. The part about the bus routes was brilliant."

For years Hana had answered compliments with "Oh, it was messy" or "I got lucky". Her counsellor had suggested an experiment: say thank you, and nothing else. So she did. "Thank you, Jamal." Then she stood there, feeling strangely exposed.

"You're welcome," Jamal said, and walked off. Nobody laughed. Nothing bad happened.

That night she opened the note on her phone called "Evidence". It had eleven lines: finished the degree, got the job, the client email that said "excellent". She added a twelfth: "Jamal, bus routes, brilliant."

When she read it, her doubt was still there, quietly muttering. But it had less room.

qa.q: Which part of the presentation did Jamal praise?
qa.a: Jamal praised the part about the bus routes.

qa.q: How did Hana feel after saying only "Thank you"?
qa.a: Hana felt awkward and exposed, but nothing bad happened.

qa.q: How does Hana's "Evidence" note support her confidence?
qa.a: It collects real achievements, so doubt has less room and good things are allowed to count.

qa.q: How might Jamal have experienced Hana's simple "Thank you"?

At the bank's training centre in Pune, Tanuja, the coach, ran an odd exercise on the last day. Each trainee had to receive one compliment from the group and reply with exactly two words: "Thank you." No "but", no "it was nothing".

When Nirmala's turn came, a colleague said, "Your customer role-play was the calmest in the room." Nirmala's mouth opened to say, "It was just practice." She caught it. "Thank you," she said. Her voice wobbled. The room clapped.

Afterwards Tanuja handed out small diaries. "Write three wins every Friday. Big or tiny. When the doubt says you're not good enough, open it."

Nirmala's first entry: "Calmest role-play. Said thank you without adding anything." It looked strange on paper. She read it twice on the train home.

qa.q: What two words did the trainees have to reply with?
qa.a: The trainees had to reply, "Thank you."

qa.q: What did Nirmala feel when she said "Thank you"?
qa.a: Nirmala felt nervous, her voice wobbling, but let the compliment stay instead of deflecting it.

qa.q: What does Tanuja's diary add to the thank-you practice?
qa.a: Writing three wins every Friday builds a record Nirmala can open when doubt says she isn't good enough.

You once told me I answer every compliment with a reason it doesn't count. You were right, and I've been working on it.
Two things I've been doing. First: when someone says something kind, I say "thank you" and then stop talking. That's it. Last week my manager said my client report was excellent. passage: Himani, you asked how I stopped being the person who says "it's nothing" to every compliment. I'm Simran, and it wasn't magic. It was practice. At twenty-four, someone told me I was a great teacher and I said, "No, the kids are just easy." My mentor heard that and said, "Next time, just say thank you. Nothing else." So I tried. The first time, a parent thanked me at pickup, and I said "thank you" and then had to physically stop myself from adding "but." It felt so awkward, like wearing someone else's shoes. The second thing was a notebook. Every Friday I wrote down one thing that went well that week. Small things. A shy child read aloud. A tough lesson worked. After a year, I had fifty-two lines. On the days I doubt myself, I open it. I still doubt myself, honestly. But the doubt doesn't win every argument any more.

qa.q: How many lines were in Simran's notebook after a year?
qa.a: Simran had fifty-two lines.

qa.a: Simran felt awkward and uncomfortable, as if wearing someone else's shoes, and had to stop from adding "but".
